stemMd:
> The municipality's free legal-advice desk should be closed. In the three years since it opened, the number of civil claims filed by residents has risen by 40 per cent, which shows that the desk is generating litigation the courts cannot absorb.

Which of the following, if true, most weakens the argument?

options.label: A
options.textMd: The 40 per cent rise was measured against the three years immediately preceding the desk's opening.

options.label: B
options.textMd: Over the same three years the proportion of filed claims struck out as hopeless fell from a third to a twentieth.

options.label: C
options.textMd: The desk advised more residents in its third year of operation than in its first.

options.label: D
options.textMd: The desk's staff are paid less than lawyers in private practice charge for equivalent advice.

explanationMd:
Identify what the argument must establish before it can recommend closure. It needs the extra claims to be a **burden**: litigation the courts cannot absorb. It infers that from a bare count of filings, saying nothing about what those filings contain.

Option B attacks exactly that inference. If the share of claims struck out as hopeless has fallen from a third to a twentieth, then before the desk opened roughly 33 in every 100 filings were wasting the court's time, and now only 5 in 100 are. The extra claims are meritorious ones that residents were previously failing to bring, and the number of hopeless claims the court must dispose of may well have fallen in absolute terms even as total filings rose. The premise survives; the conclusion drawn from it does not.

**How to check.** Ask of each option whether the argument could still be made if the option were true. It survives D (cost is a separate question), C (more clients is what a working desk looks like, and says nothing about claim quality), and A (a sensible baseline, if anything a point in the argument's favour). It does not survive B, because B supplies a different and better explanation of the same 40 per cent — quality rising, not frivolity spreading.

distractorRationale.d: Relative staff costs bear on whether the desk is good value, not on whether it generates unabsorbable litigation. The argument never claims the desk is expensive, so contradicting a claim it did not make leaves the reasoning untouched.
distractorRationale.c: Growing use of the desk is consistent with the argument and, read uncharitably, supports it: more advice given could mean more claims filed. It offers no information about whether those claims deserve to be heard, which is the point the argument needs.
distractorRationale.a: This confirms that the comparison is being drawn against a sensible baseline rather than an arbitrary one, which shores up the premise instead of undermining it. A detail that makes a statistic more trustworthy cannot weaken an argument built on that statistic.

accessibilityText: A verbal reasoning question. An argument states that a municipality's free legal-advice desk should be closed because civil claims filed by residents have risen 40 per cent in the three years since it opened, which the argument says shows the desk generates litigation the courts cannot absorb. The question asks which of four statements, if true, most weakens the argument.

provenance.notes: Original item written to the published Bocconi Law syllabus entry on identifying the statement that most weakens or strengthens an argument. The municipality, service and figures are invented. Options were screened so that exactly one bears on the inference from claim volume to court burden.

review.author: bocconi-law-wave3-author

independentSolve.workingNotes: The argument treats the 40% rise as unwanted litigation that the desk generates. (b) shows that the share of hopeless claims fell sharply, so the extra claims look well-founded and the desk seems to be screening out weak ones. That undercuts the case for closing it. (a) only sets the baseline for the comparison and is neutral or slightly strengthening; (c) is consistent with the desk driving more filings and so tends to strengthen; (d) is irrelevant to the reasoning. (b) weakens the harmful-litigation premise more than the capacity claim itself, but it is clearly the only option that weakens.

review.notes: Author's working: the argument infers burden from volume alone, so only evidence about claim quality or court load reaches it. B does, by showing the struck-out share fell from a third to a twentieth. A is off-topic, C is neutral or mildly supportive, D supports the premise's baseline. An earlier draft offered 'claims also rose in neighbouring municipalities without a desk' as a distractor; it was removed because it is a second genuine weakener, which would have left two defensible answers.
